content: The validation of drug resistance in tuberculosis has been thoroughly established using both the resistance ratio and absolute concentration methods. Detailed methodologies and instructions for preparing commonly used egg-based media, such as Löwenstein-Jensen and Ogawa, are available in the literature. The selection of drugs for susceptibility testing depends on the objectives of the survey and logistical considerations. If the goal is to determine the burden of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), testing for susceptibility to both rifampicin and isoniazid is the minimum requirement. In settings with limited laboratory capacity, rifampicin susceptibility testing can be used as an initial screening tool. Strains resistant to rifampicin should subsequently be tested for isoniazid resistance. Given the significant challenges in treating extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB), MDR-TB strains should also be tested for susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents available in the specific setting. If the survey aims to monitor trends in drug resistance over time and recent, high-quality data on MDR-TB burden already exist, testing for rifampicin resistance alone is sufficient. This approach is discussed in greater detail in other sections of the guidelines. To ensure the reliability of drug susceptibility testing (DST) results, a comprehensive laboratory quality assurance system is essential. This system should continuously monitor internal work practices, technical procedures, equipment, and materials (internal quality control) and systematically assess laboratory capabilities through external laboratory support (external quality assessment). For molecular-based DST, a single verification test must be performed for each module upon installation of a GeneXpert instrument and after calibration of instrument modules. Each instrument should be monitored using a minimum set of indicators, such as the number of tests performed per month per module, the number and proportion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis-positive results, the number and proportion of rifampicin-resistant results, and the number and proportion of errors, indeterminate results, and invalid results. For line probe assays (LPA), negative and positive controls should be included in each run, and the success of the amplification reaction should be verified by the control zones on the testing strips. For culture-based DST, the quality of the culture medium should be controlled with each batch of isolates tested. Drugs added to the medium must be pure substances obtained from reputable sources and properly stored. Drug dilutions and their addition to the medium should follow accepted standards. Susceptibility testing should be performed on the standard H37Rv M. tuberculosis strain and a combination of strains with known resistance to two or three drugs, avoiding XDR-TB strains. Since media batches are consumed quickly, reference strains may need to be included with each batch of survey strains processed for DST. Internal quality control procedures for new batches of drug-free and drug-containing media should be applied, and results should always be validated by a supervisor to ensure that strains with doubtful results are retested. External quality assessment involves proficiency testing, retesting of strains, and onsite evaluations of laboratories, conducted in collaboration with an external partner laboratory. The Supranational Reference Laboratory Network (SRLN) plays a critical role in strengthening laboratory capacity worldwide and ensuring the accuracy of national drug resistance surveillance. SRLs maintain high quality by participating in annual intra-network proficiency testing of DST. They determine a consensus on the susceptibilities of selected strains to first-line drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) and second-line drugs (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin, ofloxacin). These strain panels are used to assess the proficiency of National Reference Laboratories (NRLs) and subnational reference laboratories that provide DST results for surveillance systems and drug resistance surveys. SRLs also provide onsite evaluations, training, and supervision as needed. Ethical considerations are paramount in anti-tuberculosis drug resistance surveys and surveillance. The overarching goal of public health activities is to promote population health, but the rights, privacy, and confidentiality of individual patients must be respected. Surveillance protocols and new systems should be reviewed by ethics committees or institutional review boards to ensure adherence to ethical standards. Key ethical principles include maintaining confidentiality, obtaining informed consent, and ensuring access to treatment. Confidentiality requires that sensitive patient information be kept private unless authorized by the individual or required for legitimate public health purposes. Informed consent should be obtained from individuals capable of making decisions or from surrogate decision-makers for incapacitated persons. However, in routine surveillance, individual informed consent may not always be feasible or appropriate, especially when population-level data are essential for achieving public health objectives. In such cases, individuals and communities should be informed about the nature and purposes of the surveillance. Access to treatment is a critical ethical issue, particularly in settings with limited capacity to treat drug-resistant TB. Test results should be communicated to patients, and those in need should be provided with appropriate treatment whenever feasible. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends treatment with second-line drugs as the standard of care for MDR-TB patients, emphasizing the cost-effectiveness of such interventions. Countries without existing MDR-TB treatment programs should establish them based on surveillance results. Conducting a drug resistance survey requires meticulous planning to ensure accurate, precise, and reliable results. The process for selecting patients must be carefully designed to obtain representative data. Measures should be in place to ensure proper categorization, validation, and quality assurance of collected data and DST results. A national coordination team, including experts in program management, laboratory techniques, and epidemiology/statistics, should oversee the survey. This team is responsible for survey preparation, coordination with SRLs, supervision, quality assurance, and final data analysis and reporting. Survey objectives must be clearly defined in the context of available resources, funding, and laboratory capacity. Special approaches may be needed to capture meaningful data for certain subgroups, such as children, prison inmates, or patients in the private health sector. A secondary aim of the survey should be to strengthen the laboratory network and enhance diagnostic capacity in the country, laying the foundation for continuous surveillance systems. The diagnostic testing algorithm should be defined in consultation with the partner SRL, considering available resources and survey objectives. Molecular methods, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, can be used as initial screening tools or alone without additional conventional methods. Culture-based methods can then be performed on resistant samples to determine the full drug susceptibility pattern. A survey protocol should outline all aspects of the survey, including roles and responsibilities, objectives, sample size, patient inclusion criteria, logistics, training, ethical considerations, laboratory testing algorithms, and quality assessment of DST results.
